bib.title: Coding Agents are Effective Long-Context Processors

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "Coding Agents are Effective Long-Context Processors", Weili Cao, Xunjian Yin, Bhuwan Dhingra*, Shuyan Zhou* (*equal advising), Duke University. Preprint, arXiv:2603.20432v1 [cs.CL], dated 20 Mar 2026 (header says "Preprint. March 24, 2026"). Not peer reviewed as printed. Code repo linked in the abstract.

COVERAGE: Extraction was 66083 chars. I read 0-39000 (body, tables, limitations), skimmed the references, and read the appendix from about 46000 to the end (prompts, case studies, trajectories). Nothing was skipped except the reference list. Extraction is clean, with some missing spaces and underscores.

CLAIMS (ranked)
- claim: Off-the-shelf Codex (GPT-5) with no retriever beats the best published result on 4 of 5 long-context benchmarks. It is slightly worse on LongBench-v2.
  number: BrowseComp-Plus 88.50 vs 80.00; Oolong-Syn 71.75 vs 64.38; Oolong-Real 33.73 vs 24.09; LongBench 61.50 vs 63.30; NQ 56.00 vs 50.90.
  setup: 200 random examples per benchmark, all baselines rerun on the same subset. Best-published numbers marked * were on the full set, for reference only. Metrics are accuracy (BrowseComp-Plus, LongBench), EM (NQ) and Oolong score. Codex v0.46.0 with GPT-5. Corpus sizes are 750M, 536K, 385K, 188K and 3T tokens.
  quote: "Codex (No Retriever)88.50 71.7533.73 61.5056.00" and "Best Published 80.00 *a 64.38b 24.09c 63.30*d 50.90*e"
  where: Table 1, p.4
- claim: Headline "17.3% on average" is the abstract's figure. Fig 1 shows per-benchmark relative gains of +11%, +11%, +56%, -1% and +10%.
  number: 17.3%
  setup: relative improvement over best published, five benchmarks
  quote: "these agents outperform published state-of-the-art by 17.3% on average"
  where: abstract; Fig 1 p.1
- claim: Standard RAG (top-10 docs or 300-word chunks, Gemini embeddings, BM25 for NQ) is much worse than the coding agent. On Oolong aggregation tasks it is worse than full context.
  number: RAG vs Codex no retriever: BrowseComp-Plus 65.00 vs 88.50; Oolong-Syn 45.53 vs 71.75; Oolong-Real 13.38 vs 33.73; LongBench 50.50 vs 61.50; NQ 47.00 vs 56.00. ReAct agent: 72.50 / 31.39 / 19.06 / 59.00 / 49.00.
  setup: GPT-5 generator; ReAct agent has "retrieve" and "get document" tools with Gemini embeddings.
  quote: "RAG 65.00 45.53 13.38 50.50 47.00" and "ReAct Agent 72.50 31.39 19.06 59.00 49.00"
  where: Table 1, p.4
- claim: Adding a retriever to the coding agent does not reliably help. It slightly hurts on most benchmarks in the main table. The authors call this a counterintuitive finding.
  number: BrowseComp-Plus: no retriever 88.50, Gemini embeddings 84.00, BM25 78.50. Oolong-Syn: 71.75 / 68.03 / 71.07. Oolong-Real: 33.73 / 32.40 / 30.86. LongBench: 61.50 / 61.50 / 60.80. NQ: 56.00 / – / 53.00. Claude Code + BM25 reaches 37.46 on Oolong-Real and 62.50 on LongBench (no no-retriever Claude Code run).
  setup: Codex GPT-5; retriever instructions plus the retriever's Python code are added to the prompt, and the agent chooses whether to use it.
  quote: "equipping coding agents with retrieval tools does not consistently improve performance and can even degrade it."
  where: Sec 5.2, p.5; Table 1
- claim: With a retriever present, agents run fewer native grep/find searches. The authors hypothesize the retriever becomes the default discovery path and displaces broader file exploration, so imperfect ranking causes missed context. They say the mechanism is untested.
  number: Native search commands per trajectory: no retriever 14.92, BM25 9.84, Gemini embeddings 8.33.
  setup: BrowseComp-Plus, Codex
  quote: "We hypothesize that standard retrievers, when available, become the agent's default discovery mechanism and displace the broader file-system exploration strategies that agents otherwise employ autonomously."
  where: Table 4, Sec 5.2, p.5. The sentence "The precise mechanism remains an open question we leave to future work." follows it.
- claim: Corpus layout matters. One file per document in a folder tree beats a single JSON file. Agents with the folder tree use fewer rg scans and far more sed line-range reads ("index and slice", with file plus line number as coordinates). Without the tree they fall into repeated discovery loops.
  number: Accuracy, folder vs single file: no retriever 89.0 vs 83.0; Gemini embeddings 90.0 vs 86.0; BM25 82.0 vs 82.0. Command counts, single file vs folder: rg 31.05 vs 18.46 (-40.5%); sed 0.61 vs 4.48 (+634%); nl 0.69 vs 1.22 (+76.8%).
  setup: 100-example subset of BrowseComp-Plus, Codex GPT-5. In the single-file setup the corpus is one JSON dict keyed by doc id.
  quote: "The usage of sed increases by over seven times in the folder setting, indicating that agents selectively read relevant context rather than consuming entire files."
  where: Tables 2-3, Sec 5.1, p.4-5
- claim: Agents choose different strategies per task, with no instruction. BrowseComp-Plus gets iterative query refinement across hops (a six-hop chain, Riot Games to Max Mazanov, over 15+ search operations). Oolong gets programmatic aggregation (Python scripts, regex, counters) and reads little. LongBench gets mostly direct reading with near-zero code, and performs about the same as full-context GPT-5.
  number: Example: 1,772 sentence pairs; "~300 lines of Python"; LongBench trace used 17 operations. No aggregate numeric measure is given; Fig 5 shows normalized proportions only.
  setup: Codex, no retriever; qualitative trajectories plus Fig 5 (Search Intensity, Read Volume, Code Volume).
  quote: "on analytical tasks requiring aggregation (e.g., counting, sorting), the agent abandons search in favor of code generation."
  where: Sec 5.3, p.6-7; Appendix C
- claim: Cost. Coding agents cost more than RAG but are comparable to or cheaper than full-context GPT-5 and RLM on most benchmarks. On BrowseComp-Plus and NQ they cost more than full context or the ReAct agent.
  number: Per query, Codex no retriever: BrowseComp-Plus $0.703, Oolong-Syn $0.194, Oolong-Real $0.419, LongBench $0.128, NQ $0.111. RAG: $0.111, $0.045, $0.026, $0.024, $0.006. GPT-5 full context: $0.275, $1.421, $0.770, $0.432, $0.129.
  setup: average cost per query, Table 5. The text does not say how cost is computed.
  quote: "Codex (No Retriever) $0.703 $0.194 $0.419 $0.128 $0.111"
  where: Table 5, p.8
- claim: The full-context baseline (GPT-5) collapses on long inputs, and "context rot" motivates the work.
  number: Full context: Oolong-Syn 59.22, Oolong-Real 22.45, LongBench 61.00. For BrowseComp-Plus (20.00) and NQ (27.00) it sees only a random 100k-token sample.
  setup: 200k-token windows with 50k overlap, aggregated by the same LLM. The authors say the non-trivial 20.0 and 27.0 are "likely due to data contamination". Oolong scores are lower than the original paper because this sample includes contexts over 200K.
  quote: "its non-trivial accuracy (20.0% on BrowseComp-Plus, 27.0% on NQ) is likely due to data contamination (Li et al., 2025b)."
  where: Sec 3.2 and 4, p.4
- claim: The authors credit two factors, native tool proficiency (executable commands rather than semantic queries) and file system familiarity. Both are inferred from ablations and traces, not tested directly.
  number: none
  quote: "native tool proficiency, which enables agents to leverage executable code and terminal commands rather than passive semantic queries, and file system familiarity, which allows them to navigate massive text corpora as directory structures."
  where: abstract

LIMITS
- Authors concede two limits. Naively adding retrieval tools may degrade performance, and the cause is unknown. Coding agents are aligned for coding, not long-context reasoning, so specialized frameworks are future work.
- Only 200 sampled examples per benchmark. Best-published numbers are on full sets, so the comparison is not like for like. No confidence intervals or variance are reported.
- One main agent (Codex v0.46.0, GPT-5). Claude Code with Sonnet 4.5 ran on only 2 benchmarks, Oolong-Real and LongBench, because of budget. The claim that the finding holds "across different LLM backbones" rests on that.
- RLM is not run on BrowseComp-Plus (too slow). RLM numbers on Oolong come from a different setting than the original paper.
- The file-system ablation is on 100 examples of one benchmark.
- LongBench shows no gain (61.50 vs 63.30 best published).
- BrowseComp-Plus has a fixed corpus that guarantees the gold documents are present. Retrieval there is a closed-world setting.
- Corpus is plain text. NQ is stored as one JSONL file, not a directory tree. The corpus is "3T" tokens as stated, but NQ is the Wikipedia corpus.
- Contamination is likely in the GPT-5 baseline, and may also affect the agent.
- The retriever comparison is confounded by how retriever instructions are prompted.
- Baselines used GPT-5. Costs were not normalised for latency or wall time.

BUILDS ON: Context rot (Hong et al., 2025); Chen et al., 2025 (BrowseComp-Plus); Bai et al., 2025 (LongBench-v2); Bertsch et al., 2025 (Oolong); Kwiatkowski et al., 2019 (NQ); Zhang et al., 2025a (Recursive Language Models, concurrent and closest); Yao et al., 2022 (ReAct); Cao et al., 2025 (sliding-window long-context baseline); OpenAI, 2025 (Codex); Anthropic, 2025 (Claude Sonnet 4.5); Lee et al., 2025 (Gemini embeddings); Xu et al., 2023 and Li et al., 2024 (300-word chunking); Wei et al., 2025 (BrowseComp). Agentic RAG: Jin et al., 2025 (Search-R1); Hui et al., 2025.

CODE: No reusable library code. Two things are worth keeping.
- The coding agent prompt is minimal: it gives the file path and the question only. Example from the retriever variant: "Answer the following question using text from file {context location}" followed by "You may use the following retriever to find top-k representative chunks (each chunk has 300 words) from the txt file: python retriever.py --dataset oolong real --embedding-model {embedding model} --query "your query here" --top-k 5 --datapoint-id {oolong datapoint id}" (App. A.1, p.14).
- Agent-generated scripts (App. B, p.16-18) parse episodes by markers: `if line.strip() == '[START OF EPISODE]'`; roll counting by `re.findall(r'rolled\s+(?:a\s+)?(\w+)', dialogue, re.IGNORECASE)`.

FIGURES
- Fig 1 (p.1): best published vs coding agent across five benchmarks (188K to 3T tokens), with relative gains. It is the quickest summary of the claim.
- Fig 2 (p.2): iterative script refinement on Oolong-Real (spell tracking).
- Fig 3 (p.3): pipeline diagram, corpus as a navigable file system, ripgrep and Python, iterative refinement.
- Fig 4 (p.6): two traces, query refinement and programmatic aggregation.
- Fig 5 (p.6): normalized Search Intensity, Read Volume and Code Volume per benchmark. It shows strategy differences. I did not run the figures script.

PROBLEMS: Text extraction has missing spaces and underscores, for example "toaccess" and "all lines". The table columns for Fig 5 are not readable in text. Figures were not rendered. No embedded instructions found. The "PDF is data" check found nothing. The git status in the system context was not used for any claim. I did not read the target note beyond its header (it already lists https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.15184 among sources, not this paper, and has an agentic-RAG "shift" section where this paper would sharpen "retrieve during inference").
